https://example-research.org/reports/pos.title: Why gym-goers abandon post-workout nutrition routines
https://example-research.org/reports/pos.text:
Post-workout routines report

We surveyed 1,200 people who train at least three times a week about what happens immediately after a session ends. The most common answer was that they leave quickly: respondents described the period after training as a transition rather than a destination, with onward commitments such as commuting, collecting children, or returning to work.

Among respondents who said they had stopped using a supplement they previously bought, the most frequently cited reason was not taste or price but the friction of preparing it at the point they wanted it. Several described their intent as high and their follow-through as inconsistent, and framed the gap as a logistics problem rather than a motivation problem.

Respondents who maintained a routine tended to describe it in terms of place and sequence: a specific shelf, a specific bag, a specific order of operations. Those who had lapsed described no such anchor.

Methodology: online panel, self-reported, fielded over four weeks. Self-reported behaviour is subject to recall bias and the sample skews toward urban gym members.

https://example-journal.test/articles/po.title: Portability and repeat purchase in sports nutrition
https://example-journal.test/articles/po.text:
Portability and repeat purchase

This analysis examines how packaging format relates to repeat purchase among buyers of sports nutrition products who train away from home.

Buyers who train at a commercial gym rather than at home reported carrying a bag to every session. Where a product did not fit that bag comfortably, it tended to stay at home, and products that stayed at home were re-ordered less often than products that travelled.

Interviewees described a hierarchy of bag space in which anything bulky, prone to leaking, or awkward to close was displaced by essentials. Container closure was mentioned repeatedly and unprompted: lids that could be opened one-handed were described positively, and lids that required two hands were described as an irritation.

The association reported here is correlational. The analysis does not establish that packaging format causes repeat purchase, and buyers who select portable formats may differ in other respects from those who do not.

https://example-fitness-review.test/cons.title: Training consistency: what regular lifters actually credit
https://example-fitness-review.test/cons.text:
Training consistency

We interviewed forty people who had trained consistently for more than three years about what they credited for that consistency.

Almost none of them credited intensity. The dominant theme was repetition and low decision cost: the same time of day, the same route, the same order of preparation. Several described deliberately removing choices from the routine so that no decision had to be made at a moment when motivation was low.

Supplement use, where present, was described in the same register: something kept in a fixed place and used at a fixed point, rather than something thought about.

https://example-research.org/reports/mea.title: Meal timing around resistance training: a practical overview
https://example-research.org/reports/mea.text:
Meal timing overview

This overview summarises how timing guidance around resistance training is interpreted by people who are not competitive athletes.

Interpretation varied widely. Some participants treated published timing guidance as a strict window and reported anxiety when they could not meet it; others treated the same guidance as broadly irrelevant to their goals. A middle group described adopting a rough habit rather than a precise schedule, on the basis that a habit they could keep was worth more than a schedule they could not.

The practical advice most commonly offered by the practitioners interviewed was to prioritise total daily intake and consistency over precise timing for non-athletes.

This is a narrative overview rather than a systematic review, and the practitioner interviews are not a representative sample.
